item.title: Minimax Theory for FPCA Under Discrete Observation Established
item.description:
Minimax Theory for FPCA Under Discrete Observation Established

Researchers have established new minimax optimal rates for Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) under discrete observation, resolving a theoretical gap that had remained open for over two decades regarding diverging spectral indices.

🔍 Overview

FPCA serves as a central dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis. However, the minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has lacked a precise characterization. The new work provides the first precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs.

🧩 How It Works

The study utilizes a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. The theoretical approach involves a general framework for sharp minimax analysis that separates spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations, exploiting their distinct structures. This methodology applies to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems.

Key theoretical contributions include:

  • Establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures.
  • Identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate.
  • Establishing minimax optimal rates for individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices.
  • Establishing minimax optimal rates for leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions under explicit growth and regularity conditions.

⚙️ Key Details

The optimal rates for both spectral targets reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms:

  • Spectral identification: One mechanism involved in the estimation process.
  • Nonparametric reconstruction: The second mechanism involved in the estimation process.

The interplay between these mechanisms gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. These results are derived under explicit growth and regularity conditions.

💡 Why It Matters

This work offers a new approach to nonparametric spectral estimation by clarifying how discrete sampling affects FPCA. As a downstream application, the study analyzes FPCA-based functional linear regression and shows that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

#FPCA #StatisticalTheory #FunctionalDataAnalysis #MinimaxRates #SpectralEstimation

Source: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond

item.title: New Method Uses Quantization Error for High-Dimensional Space-Filling Designs
item.description:
New Method Uses Quantization Error for High-Dimensional Space-Filling Designs

Researchers propose a new approach to space-filling design in computer experiments that replaces traditional maximin and minimax criteria with quantization error of the uniform measure on a hypercube, addressing sensitivity to boundaries and high-dimensional limitations.

🔍 Overview

  • Maximin and minimax criteria suffer major drawbacks in high dimensions.
  • Deploying space-filling designs requires extremely large numbers of design points when dimension $d$ is very large.
  • These criteria are highly sensitive to boundaries, especially vertices of a hypercube, particularly when design size is less than $2^d$.

🧩 How it works

  • Uses quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube instead of maximin or minimax criteria.
  • Quantization error accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point to the design.
  • It is less sensitive to boundary effects than maximin and minimax criteria.
  • Zador’s theorem enables a smooth transition to uniform designs as design size tends to infinity.
  • Builds on recent results on optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772).
  • Generates random designs of target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error.
  • The support of the resulting distribution constructs designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$.

⚙️ Key details

  • Designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well for moderate $n$.
  • These designs perform significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube.
  • The method explains how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

💡 Why it matters

  • Addresses the fundamental limitation of traditional space-filling criteria in high dimensions.
  • Provides a less boundary-sensitive alternative that scales naturally with design size.
  • Demonstrates practical construction using fractional factorial subsets of vertices, offering computational advantages.

#SpaceFillingDesign #QuantizationError #HighDimensions #ComputerExperiments #OptimalQuantizers

Source: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes

item.title: NOTREKS: Improving Causal Discovery with Marginal Independence
item.description:
NOTREKS: Improving Causal Discovery with Marginal Independence

A new method for causal discovery, NOTREKS, has been introduced. It incorporates prior knowledge of marginally independent pairs of variables into score-based structure learning.

🔍 Overview

  • NOTREKS information is derived from the fact that marginally independent pairs of variables cannot be connected by a trek under faithfulness.
  • The method introduces a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search.

🧩 How it works

  • NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery by restricting the search space and improving both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.
  • The method is tested on synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information.

⚙️ Key details

  • The paper is titled “NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning” and was submitted on 18 Nov 2026.
  • The method is part of the Statistics > Machine Learning category on alphaXiv.

💡 Why it matters

  • The NOTREKS method can improve causal discovery by incorporating prior knowledge of marginally independent pairs of variables.
  • It can enhance both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.

#CausalDiscovery #MachineLearning #Statistics #NOTREKS

Source: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning

item.title: Locally Adaptive Neural Networks Achieve Optimal Performance
item.description:
Locally Adaptive Neural Networks Achieve Optimal Performance

A new approach to training neural networks, called locally adaptive neural networks, has been developed. This method addresses the limitations of globally fitted neural networks, which struggle with inhomogeneous regression functions that vary rapidly in some regions and are nearly flat in others.

🔍 Overview

  • Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space.
  • In regression problems, if the regression function is inhomogeneous, no single model can be appropriate everywhere, leading to degraded performance in regions where the function varies most rapidly.

🧩 How it works

  • Instead of fitting the network globally, the new approach fits it locally.
  • For each query point, a local neural network is trained on the k nearest-neighbours of that point alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent.

⚙️ Key details

  • The performance of the resulting estimator is analyzed through a localization approach.
  • The pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of k attains the rate n^{-2α/(2α+d*)}, up to logarithmic factors, when f0 is locally α-Hölder with α∈(0,1] and the covariates are supported on a d*-dimensional manifold embedded in ℝ^d.
  • A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal.
  • However, the local rate-optimality requires k to be calibrated to the smoothness of f0, which is unknown in practice.
  • A locally adaptive choice of k is provided to make the neural network adapt to the local Hölder exponent of f0 and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously.

💡 Why it matters

  • An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper “Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive” was submitted on 17 Nov 2026.
  • It is available in the Mathematics > Statistics Theory category on arXiv.

#NeuralNetworks #MachineLearning #Statistics #DataScience

Source: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive

item.title: Rank-Induced Bias in LLM Leaderboards Can Systematically Overstate Top Model Performance
item.description:
Rank-Induced Bias in LLM Leaderboards Can Systematically Overstate Top Model Performance

Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. A new analysis reveals this “leaderboard winner’s curse” arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability — and the same selection effect distorts scores throughout the entire leaderboard, a phenomenon the authors term rank-induced bias.

🔍 The Problem

  • Reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated on public LLM leaderboards
  • Ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability
  • The same selection effect distorts scores throughout the leaderboard, not just at the top
  • Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile

🧩 How the Bootstrap Correction Works

The researchers develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap method to correct for this bias:

  • Assumes a fixed model pool with independently, identically distributed, bounded tasks
  • Allows arbitrary within-task correlation among models
  • Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, reduces $Θ(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$
  • Also quantifies confidence intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and groups models into tiers
  • Establishes sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers

⚙️ Key Results

Benchmark / Metric Finding
Scope of correction 14 benchmarks across 5 benchmark families
Magnitude of adjustment Rank-1 adjustments range from ~0.09 to 3.86 percentage points
SWE-bench Verified (tied leaders) Adjustment of 0.90 percentage points
Tier recovery (SWE-bench Verified) 13 of 173 models placed in the leading tier

Validation uses sample splitting and calibrated simulations.

🚀 Availability

The findings are combined in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER), which integrates both the score adjustment and the rank-interval tiers. The authors advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Systematic overstatement undermines confidence in leaderboard-based model comparisons
  • Even small adjustments (under 1 pp) can flip the apparent ranking of tied leaders
  • Tier-grouping gives a more honest picture of which models genuinely perform at the same level
  • Benchmark designers should account for selection effects and ranking uncertainty in future evaluations

#LLM #Leaderboards #Benchmarking #MachineLearning #Statistics #AISafety

Source: SOTA or Luck? The Winner’s Curse in LLM Leaderboards

item.title: Introduction of SCALE for Cost-Aware AI and Human Hypothesis Testing
item.description:
Introduction of SCALE for Cost-Aware AI and Human Hypothesis Testing

Researchers have developed a new framework to conduct valid hypothesis tests by combining AI judgments with selective human verification to minimize costs.

🔍 Overview

Large language models are frequently used as inexpensive judges for labeling data, evaluating outputs, and assessing quality standards. However, because AI evaluations can be noisy or biased, rigorous hypothesis testing requires the explicit control of type-I and type-II errors.

🧩 How it works

The framework considers a population of items with hidden binary labels. From a fixed pool of items, a decision maker can:

  • Selectively query AI.
  • Send an item directly to a human.
  • Escalate an AI-scored item to a human after observing the AI report.
  • Stop once sufficient evidence has accumulated.

⚙️ Key details

To implement this process, the researchers developed SCALE, a sequential cost-aware policy that combines selective AI scoring with adaptive human escalation. Key technical aspects include:

  • Information-Theoretic Lower Bound: A derivation that captures the minimum cost for prescribed testing errors and characterizes the value of human verification and AI information.
  • Validity: SCALE is valid at finite sample sizes and matches the lower bound to first order as target error probabilities vanish.
  • Adaptability: The framework can be extended to an unknown AI-output model using paired AI-human pilot data.

💡 Why it matters

Numerically, SCALE provides the largest savings when both inexpensive AI judgments and selective human verification are valuable. In cases where one source clearly dominates, the system approaches AI-only or Human-only testing.

#LLM #HypothesisTesting #AIevaluation #DataLabeling

Source: Human-AI-Powered Hypothesis Testing: Cost-Aware Selective AI Scoring and Sequential Human Escalation
